claim: Every template wraps the attribute in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`, so projects targeting netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework get generated formatters and resolvers with no attribute. The requirement asks for all generated code to be decorated, and the condition is only allowed where the attribute does not exist. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` is in the netstandard2.0 reference assemblies and in .NET Framework 4.0+, and it can be applied to classes on both. The exclusion is unnecessary and drops coverage exclusion for a large share of consumers, which do not get the attribute through the generated code.

claim: The `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard drops the attribute on targets where it already exists. `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute` has shipped since .NET Framework 4.0 and is part of netstandard2.0, and its AttributeUsage has always allowed classes. So the guard is not needed for compilation. Its only effect is that projects targeting netstandard2.0 (including Unity and multi-targeted libraries) or any .NET Framework TFM get formatters and resolvers with no ExcludeFromCodeCoverage. That breaks the criterion 'All generated code is decorated', with no setting to turn it back on. The same guard is copied into every template: formatter, string-key, enum, union, resolver, composite resolver, FormatterCache and GetFormatterHelper.

claim: The `#if`/`#endif` lines are emitted at column 0 with `\r\n` endings, and in FormatterTemplate.cs and StringKeyFormatterTemplate.cs the `#if` directly follows prior output with no leading newline. Preprocessor directives must start on their own line. This relies on the preceding Write ending in a newline. After EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces, TransformUtilities was changed to emit `{\r\n` so the directive does not land on the same line as `{`. That change affects all nested-type output, including nested-type snapshots that have constraints.
